prompt: A table has 200 columns and 4 billion rows. A query names two of those columns and no others. Roughly what fraction of the table's stored bytes must the engine touch, and what would make that estimate badly wrong?
criteria: Lands near 1 percent — two columns out of two hundred
Says the row count cancels out because every column has the same number of rows
Names unequal column widths as the reason the fraction shifts
Notes that one wide string column can dominate the byte total

prompt: A colleague defends `SELECT *` on a 90-column warehouse table by saying the database has to read the whole row off disk anyway. Take that reasoning apart.
criteria: States that storage is laid out per column, so unnamed columns are never fetched
Says `SELECT *` forces every column to be read and decompressed
Says the cost tracks the columns named rather than the width of the row
Identifies the claim as an assumption carried over from row-oriented storage

prompt: Two columns hold 4 billion values each: one is an event date that arrives roughly in order, the other is a random identifier. The date column ends up a fraction of the size on disk. What is doing the work?
options: Neighbouring values in the date column repeat or step predictably, so encodings collapse long runs
Date columns are indexed by default, and the index replaces the stored values
The identifier column is held uncompressed because it is a key
Compression is only applied to columns that appear in a WHERE clause

prompt: Which of these follow directly from storing a table one column at a time instead of one row at a time?
options: Scanning three columns of a 90-column table reads a small slice of the total bytes
Values sitting next to each other share a type and often a narrow range, so encodings pay off
Assembling one complete row by key is comparatively expensive
Adding a column means rewriting every row already stored
Summing a single numeric column can avoid touching any other column
Every query has to scan the whole table because no index can exist

prompt: Start from one sentence: system A takes thousands of tiny single-row writes a second, system B answers a few dozen enormous scans an hour. Derive from that alone why A ends up normalised with many indexes and B ends up wide and denormalised.
criteria: Ties normalisation to keeping a single-row write cheap and unduplicated
Says an index speeds point lookups but taxes every write that maintains it
Explains that a scan reading most rows gets no benefit from a B-tree index
Links denormalisation to avoiding joins across billions of rows

prompt: An engineer wants the weekly revenue rollup to query the live application database directly, to avoid the complexity of standing up a warehouse. Push back.
criteria: Names contention with live transactional traffic as the immediate risk
Says a row store must read entire rows to aggregate one column
Acknowledges the real cost the proposal is trying to avoid
Offers a concrete alternative such as a read replica or a nightly extract

prompt: Match each design choice to the access pattern that makes it pay for itself.
left: One wide table with attribute values repeated on every row
An index on each column a form lets the user filter by
Physically sorting rows by event date as they land
right: Answering an aggregate that never joins
Returning one known row in single-digit milliseconds
Changing one customer's address in exactly one place
Skipping whole blocks of a five-year table for a 7-day question

prompt: True or false: when an analytical query that scans a billion rows runs slow, adding indexes is the standard fix. Say what makes your verdict hold.
criteria: States that a query touching most rows gains nothing from an index lookup
Names partitioning, clustering or reading fewer columns as the real lever
Says indexes earn their keep on selective single-row access
Mentions the write and storage overhead each extra index adds

prompt: A product owner with no engineering background asks why you need to run and pay for a small server just to call a paid API, when the thing you built is only a web page. Answer them.
criteria: States that anything the browser downloads can be read by the person using it
Avoids jargon such as CORS, bundler or environment variable
Names the concrete risk: a stranger spending against your account
Ends on one recommendation rather than a menu of options

prompt: You ship a browser-only app that calls a paid model API with the key written into the JavaScript, and you lock the key to your own domain in the provider's console. What breaks first, and what did that domain restriction actually buy you?
criteria: Says the key is readable in the page source or the network tab
States that the origin or referrer header is sent by the client and can be forged
Names quota exhaustion or an unexpected bill as the first visible symptom
Concludes that only a server you control can hold the key

prompt: True or false: running the bundle through a minifier so the API key is not greppable in the shipped source makes it acceptable to keep the key in the browser. Justify the verdict.
criteria: States that the running code must hand the real key to the network layer
Notes the key then appears in plain text in the request headers
Says obfuscation raises the effort without moving the trust boundary
Points at the devtools network tab as where it surfaces anyway

prompt: A page served as static files needs to call a paid API. Four arrangements are proposed. Which one actually keeps the key out of the visitor's reach?
options: Fetch the key from a `config.json` sitting beside the page at startup
Inject the key at build time from an environment variable
Send the request to a server you control, which attaches the key and forwards it
Write the key into `localStorage` on first load and read it from there afterwards

prompt: A list of fifty buttons is thrown away and rebuilt from scratch whenever the data changes, yet one click handler attached once to the surrounding container keeps working on the new buttons. Explain the mechanism.
criteria: States that a click travels up from the clicked node through its ancestors
Says the handler inspects `event.target` to learn which button was hit
Explains that freshly created children need no listener of their own
Notes that the container element itself is never replaced

prompt: One delegated listener on a container is usually the move. When is a listener per element the better choice instead?
criteria: Names an event that does not bubble, such as focus or scroll
Says the delegated handler must filter targets, which breaks as markup shifts
Gives a case where a child calls `stopPropagation` and the container never hears it
Mentions a small fixed set of elements as a reason not to bother

prompt: An outer `div` and an inner `button` each get a click listener that logs its own name. Both are registered with the default options and neither calls `stopPropagation`. Someone clicks the button. What gets logged, in what order?
explain: Listeners registered without `capture` run in the bubble phase, so the innermost target fires first and the event then travels up: `button`, then `div`.

prompt: This delegated click handler never selects anything, whatever row the user clicks. Find the line at fault.
why: The click lands on the inner `<span>`, so `e.target` is that span, not the `<li>` carrying `data-id`. The handler has to walk up first: `e.target.closest('.row').dataset.id`.

prompt: A page loads its data at startup with `const data = await fetch(url).then(r => r.json())` and renders from it. Months later the file is moved and the host answers that path with its own 404 page. What breaks first, and what does the visitor see?
criteria: States that `fetch` does not reject on a 404 response
Says `r.json()` is the thing that fails, because it is handed HTML
Names an empty screen as what the visitor actually gets
Proposes checking `r.ok` before parsing the body

prompt: Review this startup path: the page fetches three separate JSON files, awaiting each one before requesting the next, with the whole block in a single `try` that logs to the console if anything throws. What would you change?
criteria: Says the three requests are independent and should overlap
Names `Promise.all` or starting all three before awaiting as the fix
Points out that a console log leaves nothing on screen for the visitor
Says one shared `try` cannot say which of the three failed

prompt: Put these steps into the order a careful on-demand JSON load performs them.
items: Swap the loading state for the rendered content
Check `response.ok` and throw with the status when it is false
Put a visible loading state on screen and call `fetch`

prompt: The network tab shows the file arriving with a 200, but the screen stays empty. One line explains it.
why: `loadBank` is `async`, so it hands back a Promise, not the parsed body. `bank.questions` is `undefined` and the render draws nothing — the call needs `await loadBank('data')` inside an async caller, or a `.then`.

prompt: A teammate wants to add a quick server-side password check to an app that lives on a static file host, saying it is only a few lines. Push back on the proposal.
criteria: States that the host runs none of your code per request
Says any check written into the page executes on the visitor's own machine
Names a concrete route such as a serverless function or a hosted auth service
Acknowledges the outcome the teammate is trying to reach

prompt: Your site is a few hundred kilobytes of HTML, CSS, JS and JSON on a static host behind a CDN, and it takes ten thousand visits a month. Estimate the monthly bill, and say what the number is made of.
criteria: Lands at or very near zero dollars a month
Multiplies page weight by visits to get a few gigabytes of transfer
Says bandwidth and stored bytes are the only meters running
Notes there is no per-request compute charge to pay at all

prompt: A static host answers each request by handing back a file from disk unchanged, running none of your ______ in the process — which is why a request for a path that does not exist comes back as a bare ______ instead of hitting a route handler.
Which of these hold for a site served by a static file host?
options: Every visitor requesting a given path receives identical bytes
Any value the page needs at run time is readable by the visitor
The host can check who is asking before it hands over a file, with nothing else added
Absorbing a traffic spike is mostly the CDN's problem rather than yours
The host can tailor the page per signed-in user before sending it
Something one visitor types can be kept for the next visitor without another service
